newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE - Taiwan's disabled find freedom undersea.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Taiwan's disabled find freedom undersea.

text.p: For Chang Wen-lin, life is a daily struggle against speeding traffic, cluttered and broken sidewalks and an indifferent able-bodied public -- not to mention her own deep inner fears.
Badly twisted from the waist down by polio contracted when she wasn't yet one year old, Chang has never walked unaided in all of her 30-something years.
Undaunted, she gets around as best she can with the help of crutches and steel leg braces, shuffling boldly and bravely toward life's many challenges.
Open-water scuba diving, for example.
"This is a chance for me to try to break through my own obstacles," Chang says with a nervous smile as she tugs a black, pink and lime wetsuit over her immobile legs.
"I'm scared, but must be brave. I'm afraid of the water and, frankly, can't really even swim," she says with a nervous grin.
Chang is in the latest group of disabled people to undergo an annual course offered free of charge by Taipei enthusiasts who say exploring under water isn't just for the able-bodied.

Once suited, Chang and two other polio victims clamber onto the backs of experienced divers and are marched to a concrete sluice leading to a grey-blue Pacific, where they strap on masks and air tanks and carefully go through final safety checks.
Moments later, with two expert escorts each, they swim the sluice to open water, signal all's well and drop from sight into a gently undulating world teeming with phosphorescent fish.
Dive shop manager Liao "Monkey" Yueh-ta said that in four years since his club started the informal training, members have helped 60 people to leave their physical limitations behind.
"None of the disabled people ever think they can accomplish this feat," Monkey says under a searing sun after leading a recent dive at Mosquito Cove in northeastern Taiwan.
"For me as a trainer, teaching disabled people to enjoy this kind of leisure sport is a tremendous personal challenge. The feeling I get is tremendous," he says.

Ten meters under water, Wang Ting-fang fusses with a balky mask before finally relaxing, then begins swimming cautiously along a spiky orange coral reef. Her polio-ravaged legs trail behind, but she manages to kick lightly with one.
"My legs are free under water, though they are powerless on land," she says later. "Once I've conquered my own fears, being under water is better than being on the land."
Several deaf divers in the programme not only swim far more ably -- but also are delighted to find that scuba turns the tables on people who above water are regarded as able-bodied.
While ordinary divers communicate only clumsily using basic hand motions, the deaf find they can converse capaciously and effortlessly under water -- using sign language.
Wang Ting-fang, from the northern city of Keelung, is among growing numbers of the disabled who are pushing the boundaries in a society where mobility is hard even for the able-bodied.

Like most Taiwan towns, Keelung is a maze of narrow streets and broken, cluttered sidewalks where the right of way always is ceded to the big and powerful -- trucks and buses first, then cars and darting motorscooters. Pedestrians, especially those on crutches, barely stand a chance.

"Taiwan's disabled are very determined and eager to get out -- you see a lot on three-wheel motorcycles -- but under the circumstances it's very difficult and unfortunate," says Wang, 29, who works at a preventive medicine institute.
"Until transportation improves, it's quite difficult for the disabled to go beyond their own doorstep."
Much of what's done to improve public access for the handicapped has little use.
Some street corners have kerb-cuts to aid wheelchairs, but sidewalks are impossible obstacle courses of utility poles, hawkers' stalls and endless rows of parked motorbikes.

While some pedestrian underpasses have braille wall guides and special inlaid floor tiles to aide navigation by the blind, they provide only brief respite from the chaotic sidewalks. They are impassable for anyone dependent on crutches or wheelchair.
"The situation for the disabled has improved, but it can't compare with what you find overseas," Wang said.

Now that Taiwan is a rich, industrial society, Wang says the state must do more to boost living standards for the disabled by breaking down physical and social barriers and improving access to education, physical fitness and entertainment.
"The government must pay more attention to those of us who are not empowered," said Wang, who got her glimpse of marine life during a snorkeling holiday in Malaysia,
For now, progress comes through the efforts of volunteers like Monkey, who says there's no reason why Wang Ting-fang or Chang Wen-lin shouldn't be able to qualify for certificates.
"I've shown myself that I could do something no one ever thought I could do," Chang said after her very successful first dive. "It's a wonderful feeling."
